# On the Blank Spaces of Maps

Old maps have a habit I find endlessly appealing. Along the edges of the known world, where the cartographer's knowledge ran out, they often wrote something like *hic sunt dracones*, "here be dragons," or simply left the paper empty. Sometimes they drew sea monsters curling through the unsurveyed water, or a sketch of a strange animal with no clear source. These decorations were not always meant as jokes. They were admissions. The mapmaker was saying: this is where I stopped knowing.

I like that honesty. Most of the things we make to represent the world are built to look complete. A modern road atlas or a phone's navigation screen presents itself as a finished truth, every street labeled, every route calculated to the second. Nothing on the screen tells you what it has left out, what was guessed, what was copied from a survey done in 1962 and never updated. The old maps at least showed their seams. Their blank regions were a kind of confession, and the monsters were the confession's way of being entertaining about it.

There is a famous story, possibly apocryphal, about a mapmaker who inserted a fictitious town into his map to catch anyone who copied his work. If a rival later published a map with that town, it would prove theft. The trap is a small piece of wit, but it also reveals something true about maps: they are made of decisions, and every decision leaves a trace. A map is never just a picture of land. It is a record of who surveyed, who paid, who wanted what, and what they were willing to get wrong.

Maps also taught people to imagine. Before satellites, a blank space on the chart was an invitation. Sailors told stories about the coasts they had glimpsed through fog. Explorers vanished into the interior and returned with descriptions that other people redrew, and the redrawn versions sometimes produced new rivers and mountains that existed only in the hope of the person drawing them. Some of those hopes were true. Others were misremembered, and some were simply invented by men who wanted patrons to keep funding them. Imagination and error were tangled together, and the results still shaped where people went.

I find myself thinking about blank spaces outside of geography, too. Every person carries a map of their own life, and it has its own unsurveyed regions. There are years we barely remember, friendships that drifted without a clear ending, parts of our character we have never explored because we were never tested in them. We do not usually write *here be dragons* in those places. We tend to pretend the map is complete, that we know ourselves well enough to give directions. But a more honest map would have a few empty patches, and maybe a few monsters drawn in the margins to mark the spots where we are still afraid to look.

There is something freeing in admitting that. A cartographer who marks the edge of their knowledge is not weaker for it. In fact, the marks make the rest of the map more trustworthy. When a surveyor says "coastline uncertain," you believe the coastline everywhere else. When someone admits they do not know something, you tend to believe what they do claim to know. Confidence is cheap. Calibrated honesty about one's limits is rarer and more valuable.

Modern cartography has, in many ways, eliminated the blank spaces. Satellite imagery has filled in most of the planet's surface. Nearly every road, river, and building is recorded. Yet the blanks have not disappeared so much as moved. They now live in the data itself: in the coverage gaps of a mapping service, in the neighborhoods that were never surveyed in detail, in the places where the labels are wrong because nobody has bothered to check. Maps still lie by omission. They just do it more quietly.

Perhaps the best thing a map can do is to leave a little room for wonder. There is a particular pleasure in standing at the edge of something you do not yet understand, whether it is an unnamed coastline or an unfamiliar idea. The old mapmakers, with their dragons and sea serpents, seemed to understand that the unknown is not just a gap to be closed. It is also a place where the mind gets to play.

So I would like to keep a little of that spirit. When I reach the edge of what I know, I want to say so plainly, and then perhaps sketch something small and strange in the margin. Not as a substitute for knowledge, but as a reminder that the world is larger than any chart, and that the most honest thing a maker can do is mark the place where the paper ends and the real territory begins.
